title: Is your attention the most valuable thing your company owns?
deck: Yes, and almost nobody puts it on the balance sheet. Every strategy, every tool, every transformation runs on the same scarce input: people's focused attention. The companies that hoard it, by killing meetings, notifications, and priorities that don't matter, out-think the ones that spend it on everything. Focus is the last competitive advantage a machine can't buy you.
metaDescription: Yes, and almost nobody puts it on the balance sheet. Every strategy, every tool, every transformation runs on the same scarce input: people's focused.

body.x: Here's a question I ask leadership teams.
What's the first thing your people do in the morning?
Nobody knows. But I do. They pick up the phone. Before coffee, before a thought of their own, they let someone else's feed set the pattern for the day.
I write in my next book about what that habit does. Start the day with the feed and you've told your pattern-seeking brain that the feed comes first. You'll go back to the trough all day.
Now multiply that by your entire company.
What's the pattern?

Every era has one scarce resource that the winners figured out first. Land, in the agrarian age. Energy, in the industrial one. Information, when the internet arrived, until information became free and infinite.

What's scarce now is attention. The ability to focus on one hard thing long enough to solve it. Every platform you use is engineered to take it, and most companies then spend whatever's left on Slack, back-to-back meetings, and eleven priorities that are all number one.
Old attention economy joke: if you're not paying for the product, you are the product. Inside a company it's worse. You're paying people for their attention and then giving it away for free.

The three defenses I write about for the individual mind are focus, discernment, and innovation. They're the same three for an organization. Where does attention go? What gets in? What new thing can we make with what's left?
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Audit attention like money. For one week, count the hours your best people spend in meetings and messages versus on actual work. The number will scare you. Good.
Protect one block a day. No meetings, no pings, for everyone, at the same time. Companies that do this describe it like discovering an extra day in the week.
And declare one priority. Not three, one. Attention can only go to one place at a time, and that's what a priority is for.
Your competitors can buy the same AI you can. They can't buy a focused team. That's still yours, if you keep it.
Where does your attention actually go before nine a.m.?

title: Is off-grid the future, or a fantasy?
deck: Neither. It's a preview. I spent a year living off-grid, and the lesson wasn't that everyone should. It's that the technologies that make it possible, solar, batteries, satellite internet, local water, are the same ones rewiring the grid itself. The future isn't everyone in the jungle. It's a grid that works more like the jungle did: local, resilient, and yours.
metaDescription: Neither. It's a preview. I spent a year living off-grid, and the lesson wasn't that everyone should. It's that the technologies that make it possible…

body.x: I spent a year living off-grid.
Two outfits, both merino wool. Solar for power. A connection to the outside world that worked when the sky was clear. Water I had to think about. A rhythm set by sunrise instead of a calendar app.
I write about that year in my next book, because it did something to my attention that no app ever has. But that's not the point of this post. The point is what it taught me about infrastructure.
What's the pattern?
Every big system starts centralized and ends distributed.

Computing began with mainframes in guarded rooms. Now it's in your pocket. Media began with three networks. Now it's everyone. Power began, and mostly still is, a handful of giant plants pushing electricity one way down long wires.

That's changing, and the technologies doing it are the ones I lived on. A solar panel on a roof. A battery in a garage. A satellite dish that turns any hillside into an office. Each one takes a piece of the grid and moves it to the edge.

Off-grid living was the extreme test case. It proved the pieces work. The interesting future isn't a million people copying me. It's those pieces stitched back into the grid: rooftops feeding batteries feeding neighborhoods, so that when the big wire fails, the small ones don't.
Texas found out what a centralized grid does under stress in February 2021. Homes with their own solar and storage were the ones with lights on.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things. Especially if you run anything that depends on the grid staying up.
Ask how long you'd last if the wire went dead. A day? An hour? That number is your resilience, and most organizations have never measured it.
Move one thing to the edge. A battery, a generator, a solar array on the warehouse. Not to leave the grid. To have a second answer.

And watch the regulation. The rules for selling power back, for microgrids, for who owns a battery in a building, are being written now. The organizations in those rooms will shape a grid that works for them.
I came back from the jungle. But the jungle taught me what the future grid looks like: not one giant thing you depend on, but many small things you can trust.
If your power went out tomorrow, what would still work?

title: What are you encrypting today that must stay secret in 2035?
deck: More than you think. Adversaries are already harvesting encrypted data to decrypt later, once quantum computers can, most likely in the 2030s. Health records, government files, trade secrets: anything still valuable in ten years is exposed now. The standards to protect it have existed since 2024. Migrate what has the longest shelf life first.
metaDescription: More than you think. Adversaries are harvesting encrypted data to decrypt once quantum computers can. Migrate what has the longest shelf life first.

body.x: Here's the wrong question: when will a quantum computer break today's encryption?
Here's the right one: how much of what you encrypted this year still needs to be secret in 2035?
What's the pattern?

Remember Y2K? Two-digit years in old software. Nothing broke on January 1, 2000, and people called it a hoax. It wasn't. It was the largest coordinated repair job in computing history, done quietly and early, which is exactly why nothing broke.
That's the pattern for quantum. Not a bang. A migration.

The threat is real but slow. To break the encryption most of the internet uses, you'd need a quantum computer with millions of stable qubits. Today's best have on the order of hundreds to low thousands, and they're noisy. Most serious estimates put a cryptographically relevant machine somewhere in the 2030s, and estimates keep moving.

But there's a twist that makes the date irrelevant. It's called harvest now, decrypt later. An adversary that records your encrypted traffic today doesn't need to break it today. They store it and wait. Health records, government files, trade secrets, anything that's still valuable in ten years is already exposed if it moved over the network this year.

In August 2024, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology published the first three post-quantum encryption standards. The math to defend against this exists and is approved. The remaining problem is the same as Y2K: finding every place the old thing lives and replacing it.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Inventory your cryptography. Most organizations don't know where their encryption lives. That inventory is step one, and it takes months, so start.
Sort your data by shelf life. What needs to be secret in 2035? Migrate that first. What's worthless next week can wait.
And ask your vendors. Every cloud, every device, every piece of software you rely on has a post-quantum plan or doesn't. Ask in writing.
Y2K was a success story people mistook for a hoax. Quantum can be the same, if we do the boring work early.
What's in your systems today that still needs to be secret in ten years?

title: Why do smart organizations keep making the same change twice?
deck: Because they never wrote down why the first one failed. Organizations keep records of what they decided and almost none of what they learned. So every few years a new leader rediscovers the same idea, runs into the same wall, and calls it new. The fix is not better memory. It's a habit of naming the pattern out loud.
metaDescription: Because they never wrote down why the first one failed. Organizations keep records of what they decided and almost none of what they learned.

body.x: Here's a scene I've watched in a dozen companies.
A new leader arrives. She sees the obvious problem. She proposes the obvious fix: centralize it, or decentralize it, depending on the year.
Someone older in the room goes quiet. Because they did exactly this in 2017. And it didn't take.
But nobody says so. And the change runs again.
What's the pattern?

Organizations swing. Centralize, decentralize. Build in-house, outsource. Open floor plan, offices again. If you've been anywhere longer than a decade, you've watched the pendulum go both ways and heard each swing described as a revolution.

The pendulum isn't the problem. Sometimes the answer really does change with the times. The problem is amnesia. Companies keep exquisite records of decisions: the memo, the org chart, the budget. They keep almost no record of lessons: why it stalled, who resisted and why, what it would have taken to work.
So the lesson leaves the building with the person who learned it.

I say on stage that change has a pattern, and that five thousand years of it repeat. That's true for civilizations. It's also true, on a smaller clock, inside your company. The same change comes around every seven or eight years, roughly the tenure of one leadership team. And each time, it arrives without its history.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Before any big change, ask one question in the open: "Have we tried this before?" Then let the quiet person answer. That's the cheapest research you will ever do.

Write the lesson, not just the decision. One page, kept somewhere people can find it: what we tried, what happened, what we'd do differently. Not a post-mortem nobody reads. A note to the next leader.
And keep one person whose job is remembering. Every organization needs an anthropologist. Someone who knows the stories, and is allowed to tell them in the room where decisions get made.
Making the same change twice isn't stupidity. It's what happens when a smart organization forgets on purpose. You can stop forgetting.
What's the change your company has already tried once, and is about to try again?

title: Can you insure against a deepfake?
deck: You can, and the market is being invented right now. Insurance has always shown up shortly after a new risk becomes common, from shipwrecks to cyberattacks. Deepfake fraud crossed that line in 2024. Policies exist but they're narrow, exclusions are wide, and the price will depend on one thing: whether you can prove your people were trained to pause.
metaDescription: You can, and the market is being invented right now. Insurance has always shown up shortly after a new risk becomes common, from shipwrecks to.

body.x: In the 1680s, a coffee house on Tower Street in London became the place ship owners went to find someone who'd bet on their cargo arriving.

That coffee house was Lloyd's. It became the insurance market that still bears the name. Insurance didn't create shipping. It showed up when shipping got common enough, and dangerous enough, that people needed to share the risk.
That's the pattern. First the risk becomes routine. Then the market prices it.
What's the pattern?

Cyber insurance ran the same script. Almost nobody had it in 2005. By the mid-2010s, after a decade of breaches, it was a normal line item. Then ransomware exploded, losses spiked, and insurers reacted the way they always do: raised prices, tightened terms, and started demanding proof that you'd done the basics. Multifactor authentication became a condition of coverage.

Deepfakes are now at the 2015 stage of that curve. The Arup case in early 2024, where a finance employee wired about $25 million after a video call full of fake colleagues, was the moment it stopped being a novelty. Insurers noticed. Some policies now name deepfake-enabled fraud. Many still exclude it, or fold it into social engineering coverage with low limits.

Here's what I expect. Within a few years, the question insurers ask won't be whether you have deepfake detection software. It'll be whether your people are trained to verify. Just as they now ask about multifactor authentication. The human pause will become a condition of coverage.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Read your policy for the words "social engineering" and "voluntary transfer." That's where deepfake losses land, and where the limits are usually smallest.
Document your verification rule. A written policy that any request to move money is confirmed on a second channel is both your best defense and your best evidence.
And train it, then log the training. Insurers underwrite what they can see. A record of people practicing the pause is worth more than any detector.
Lloyd's started in a coffee house because ships kept sinking. This market is starting because faces can be faked. The response is the same: share the risk, and prove you did the basics.
Does your policy cover the day someone with your CFO's face asks for a wire?

title: Is perception the new battlefield?
deck: It always was. What changed is that the weapons are cheap. Every war has been fought partly over what people believe is true, but now anyone can manufacture a convincing reality for the price of a subscription. The defense isn't a better detector. It's a population that knows how its own perception can be hijacked.
metaDescription: It always was. What changed is that the weapons are cheap. Every war has been fought partly over what people believe is true, but now anyone can.

body.x: In 2024, a finance employee at the engineering firm Arup joined a video call with his chief financial officer and several colleagues.
They asked him to make a series of transfers. He did. About $25 million.
Everyone on that call except him was a deepfake.
What's the pattern?

Perception has been a battlefield for as long as there have been armies. The Trojan horse was a perception attack. So was every forged letter, every planted rumor, every propaganda leaflet dropped from a plane. Sun Tzu wrote that all warfare is based on deception, twenty-five centuries ago.

What changed is the cost. Faking a person used to take a studio, a team, and weeks. Now it takes a laptop and an afternoon. When the cost of manufacturing reality drops to near zero, the volume goes up, and the target stops being generals. It's everyone. Your finance team. Your parents. You.

I've spent the last few years thinking about this under a name I use: perceptual security. Cybersecurity protects the machine. Perceptual security protects the human looking at it. And right now we spend billions on the first and almost nothing on the second.

In my next book I write about the three defenses: focus, discernment, and innovation. The Arup employee didn't lack technology. He lacked a moment of pause, and a culture that made it normal to say "let me call you back on a number I trust."
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Build the pause in. Any request that moves money or data gets verified on a second channel, every time, no matter who appears to be asking. Make it a rule so nobody has to be brave.
Train perception, not just passwords. Show your people what a deepfake looks like today. Then remind them it will look better tomorrow.
And treat discernment as a skill you hire and promote for. The person who says "something feels off" is the most valuable sensor you own. Reward them for saying it, even when they're wrong.
The battlefield was always perception. We just used to have more time. Now the time is what you have to build yourself.
When did you last verify a request that looked completely normal?

title: Does change fatigue exist, or is it change without a pattern?
deck: Both, but the second one is the one you can fix. People aren't tired of change. They're tired of change that arrives with no shape: another tool, another reorg, another priority, none of it connected. Give people the pattern and the same amount of change feels lighter, because now they can see where it's going.
metaDescription: Both, but the second one is the one you can fix. People aren't tired of change. They're tired of change that arrives with no shape: another tool, another…

body.x: Everyone's talking about change fatigue.

Gartner has been measuring it for years. Employees' willingness to support organizational change has dropped sharply over the last decade; in Gartner's surveys it fell from about three quarters of employees in 2016 to under half in 2022.
So yes, it's real. But I think we're naming it wrong.
What's the pattern?

In my next book I write about what a constant feed does to a human nervous system. It isn't the volume of information that wears you down. It's information with no pattern. Random pings, out of order, each one demanding a reaction. That's what a brain can't rest inside.
Work has become the same feed. A new platform in March. A reorg in June. A new strategy in the fall, with a new word for it. None of it connected. Each one presented as the thing that matters now.
What people call change fatigue is mostly pattern fatigue. The brain is a pattern-seeking instrument. Give it a shape and it can carry a lot. Deny it a shape and even small things exhaust it.

I've watched teams absorb enormous change without complaint, because someone drew the map. "This is where we are. This is where we're going. These three moves are the same journey." And I've watched teams collapse under a fraction of that, because every change came from nowhere.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.

Connect every change to the one story. If you can't say how the new tool relates to the new strategy relates to the reorg, don't launch it yet. Not because the change is wrong, but because unconnected change costs more than it returns.
Stop announcing. Start locating. Instead of "we're launching X," say "we're at step three of five, and this is step three." People can rest inside a sequence.
And cut one thing for every thing you add. Fatigue also comes from nothing ever ending. Name what's over.
Change has a pattern. When people can see it, they stop being tired of it and start steering it.
What's the map your team is missing?
*Related: [What year is it inside your company?](/writing/what-year-is-it-inside-your-company)*

title: Will AI's power bill decide who wins the next decade?
deck: Yes. Every technology era is decided by who controls the energy underneath it, and AI is the hungriest one yet. Data centers used about as much electricity as Japan in 2024, and the demand is set to more than double by 2030. The countries and companies that can generate, store, and move that power will set the terms. The rest will rent.
metaDescription: Yes. Every technology era is decided by who controls the energy underneath it, and AI is the hungriest one yet.

body.x: Let's talk about the part of AI nobody wants on a slide.

The International Energy Agency estimated that data centers consumed around 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, roughly one and a half percent of the world's total. Their projection: about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, more than doubling, with AI the main driver.
That's about the electricity use of Japan, on its way to more.
What's the pattern?
Here's what history says. Every era runs on an energy source, and whoever controls it writes the rules.

Coal built the British Empire. Oil built the American century. In Radical Next I write about the Kardashev scale, the physicist Nikolai Kardashev's idea that a civilization's advancement can be measured by how much energy it can harness. He was thinking about stars. But the logic works at the scale of nations and companies too.

The next era's energy question isn't just how much. It's where, how fast, and how clean. Chip wars are really energy wars. Data center sites are chosen by grid capacity before anything else. Countries with cheap, reliable power are becoming the new resource states, and countries without it are becoming customers.
And there's a second-order effect. When compute costs are dominated by electricity, the price of thinking becomes the price of power. That reshapes who gets to build, and where.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Know your AI's energy footprint before your board asks. It's coming as a question and a cost line.
Treat power as strategy. If your operations depend on compute, your energy contracts are now part of your competitive position. Most companies leave that to facilities.

And watch the grid, not just the model. The bottleneck of the next five years isn't chips. It's transformers, transmission lines, and permits. The organizations moving early on those will have compute when others are waiting.
Every era has an energy question. This one arrived faster than the last, and it's already on your bill.
Do you know what your AI cost you in electricity last month?

title: Is "AI-free" about to become a selling point?
deck: Yes, and it will follow the path organic food took. First a fringe claim, then a premium, then a regulated label. When most content, products, and service are machine-made, human-made becomes a signal worth paying for. The brands that can prove it, not just say it, will own the top of the market.
metaDescription: Yes, and it will follow the path organic food took. First a fringe claim, then a premium, then a regulated label.

body.x: I'll tell you where this is going by telling you where it's been.

In 1990, the United States passed the Organic Foods Production Act. Before that, "organic" was a word anyone could put on a carrot. Farmers who meant it were competing with farmers who didn't, and shoppers couldn't tell the difference.
So the word got a standard. And then it got a price.
Organic went from a co-op bin to a $70 billion market. Not because organic food changed. Because the label became provable.
What's the pattern?

Every time a technology makes something abundant, the scarce version gets a name and a premium. Machine-woven cloth made "handmade" valuable. Factory food made "artisanal" a word on a menu. Mass photography made "original print" a market.

Now the machine can make everything: the product description, the customer service reply, the song, the image, the article. Pew found that over a third of web pages published since ChatGPT launched show signs of AI authorship. That's the abundance.
So "made by a human" is becoming the label. Some brands already use it. Right now it's unregulated, like organic in 1989. Anyone can claim it.
That won't last. The claim will get contested, then standardized, then certified. And at that point it stops being marketing and starts being a real market.

I said in Radical Next that the Great Flattening, the reversion to the bland mean, is the risk of a world that trains on itself. The other side of that risk is opportunity. The human version becomes the thing worth choosing.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Decide where you're human on purpose. Not everywhere; that's not honest and not affordable. The parts that matter: the design, the service moment, the words with your name on them.
Make it provable before someone makes you. A real person's name, a real photo, a process you can describe. When the standard arrives, be the brand that already meets it.
And don't fake it. The organic market had its scandals. Brands caught claiming human-made when it wasn't will lose more than they gained.
The label is coming. The only question is whether your brand is the one that earns it or the one that gets caught.
What would your customers pay more for, if they knew a person made it?
*Related: [When your customer is a bot, what is a brand?](/writing/when-your-customer-is-a-bot-what-is-a-brand)*

title: Can a team stay human through a reorg?
deck: Yes, if you protect the one thing a reorg always breaks first: the small circle of people who actually trust each other. Org charts change in a day. Trust takes years. Most restructures redraw the boxes and forget the lines between them. Keep the lines, and people will follow you through almost any set of boxes.
metaDescription: Yes, if you protect the one thing a reorg always breaks first: the small circle of people who actually trust each other. Org charts change in a day.

body.x: Every reorg starts with a slide.
Boxes move. Names move. Someone gets a dotted line. And in the room where the slide gets made, it looks like a clean solution.
Then it lands on the floor, and something goes quiet.
What's the pattern?

For most of the million years we've been human, we lived in groups of about 150. That number has a name now, Dunbar's number, after the anthropologist Robin Dunbar, who found that our brains seem to top out at roughly 150 stable relationships. Inside that circle, you know who to trust because you've watched them. Bad apples are hard to hide. Debts get settled face to face.
I wrote about this in Radical Next, because it's the original operating system for trust. Localized. Direct. Earned.

Companies are much bigger than 150. But look closely and you'll see they still run on circles of about that size, and inside those on circles of five or ten. The people who cover for you. The ones you'd call at midnight. That's the real org chart, and it never appears on the slide.
A reorg redraws the boxes. Trust lives in the lines. Break enough lines at once and you don't have a new structure. You have strangers with new titles.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.

Map the lines before you move the boxes. Ask each team who they actually depend on. Then try not to sever more than one of those ties per person. That single constraint saves more reorgs than any change-management deck.
Move circles, not individuals. If a group works, move it together. Splitting a working five to seed five new teams sounds efficient. It usually just kills the one team that worked.
And give people a reason they can repeat. "Why are we doing this?" will be asked in every hallway. If the answer takes a slide, it will be replaced by a rumor by lunch.
People have survived far bigger changes than a restructure. They did it in small circles that held. Keep the circles.
Which line on your team would you never want to cut?
*Related: [What year is it inside your company?](/writing/what-year-is-it-inside-your-company)*

title: Why is the robot still waiting on the human?
deck: Because the hard part was never the thinking. It was the hands. Robots can beat us at chess and can't fold laundry. That's called Moravec's paradox and it's been true since 1988. Factories that tried to remove the human found the robot waiting for a person to fix the one thing it couldn't. The winning design puts the two together.
metaDescription: Because the hard part was never the thinking. It was the hands. Robots can beat us at chess and can't fold laundry.

body.x: In 2018, Tesla was trying to build the Model 3 at a rate the industry called impossible.

It was failing. Elon Musk had built one of the most automated car factories in the world, and the line kept stopping. In April, he admitted on Twitter that excessive automation had been a mistake. His exact words: humans are underrated.
The most automated factory on earth was waiting on the humans.
What's the pattern?

In 1988, the roboticist Hans Moravec noticed something strange. The things we think of as hard, calculus, chess, logic, are easy for machines. The things we think of as easy, walking across a room, picking up an egg, noticing that a part is slightly wrong, are enormously hard.
The reason is evolutionary. We've had a billion years to perfect perception and movement. We've had a few thousand years of abstract reasoning, so it's shallow, and easy to copy.

That's Moravec's paradox, and it's the reason the robot is still waiting. Every factory that tried to go fully dark hit the same wall: the machine could do ten thousand identical motions and then stop, helpless, at the one part that came in slightly bent.

The pattern shows up in every era. Steam didn't remove the machinist. Electricity didn't remove the line worker. Each one changed what the human did and made the remaining human work more valuable, not less.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.

Automate the identical, not the variable. Anything that happens the same way ten thousand times, give to the machine. Anything that varies, keep a person nearby, and design the job so the machine hands off gracefully instead of stopping.
Measure the handoff. The productivity of a modern line lives at the moment the robot needs a human. Make that fast, obvious, and dignified.
And pay for perception. The worker who notices the bent part before the line stops is worth more than the robot. Most pay scales say otherwise. Fix that.
Humans are underrated. Tesla learned it the expensive way. You don't have to.
Where in your operation is the machine waiting on a person, and how long does it wait?
*Related: [How do you get employees to adopt change they didn't ask for?](/writing/how-do-you-get-employees-to-adopt-change-they-didnt-ask-for)*

title: Who is accountable when your bank's AI says no?
deck: The bank is, and the law already says so. Since 1974, a lender in the United States has had to tell you why it turned you down. That rule didn't anticipate machine learning, but it applies to it. The question isn't whether AI can say no. It's whether anyone at the bank can explain why, in a sentence a human could act on.
metaDescription: The bank is, and the law already says so. Since 1974, a lender in the United States has had to tell you why it turned you down.

body.x: Picture the letter.
Your loan was declined. The reason, in the language regulators now warn against, is that the model said so.
That letter is illegal. And it's been illegal for fifty years.
What's the pattern?

In 1974, the United States passed the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. It was written for a world where a loan officer could look at a woman and decide she needed her husband's signature. Among other things, it required lenders to give a specific reason when they said no. Not "insufficient credit." The actual factors.
That reason requirement, the adverse action notice, is the part that matters now.

Because the model can absolutely say no. It can say it faster and more consistently than any loan officer. What it often can't do is say why, in a way that means anything to the applicant. And in 2023, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau made it explicit: a complex algorithm is not an excuse. If you use it, you still owe the reason.

Every era of automation in finance has run into this. The credit score itself faced it in the 1990s. Regulators didn't ban the score. They required that it could be explained. The same will happen here. The banks that build the explanation in early will move fast. The ones that bolt it on later will pay for it in enforcement.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Make "explain the no" a design requirement, not a compliance afterthought. If the model can't produce a reason a person could act on, it isn't finished.
Name the human. For every automated decision that affects a customer, one person should be accountable for the outcome. Not a committee. A name.

And test for the answer you'd be embarrassed by. Run your declines through one question: would we be comfortable reading this reason aloud to the customer? If not, the model isn't the problem. The silence is.
Accountability didn't get harder when the machine arrived. The rule was always the same. Say why.
Could your bank explain its last hundred declines in one sentence each?
*Related: [Would you let an AI agent spend your money?](/writing/would-you-let-an-ai-agent-spend-your-money)*

title: Should leaders tell the truth about how hard the next year will be?
deck: Yes. People can handle a hard truth far better than a soft lie they'll discover in six months. What they can't handle is not knowing what's real. The leaders people follow through the worst years are the ones who said the worst part out loud, and then said what we do next.
metaDescription: Yes. People can handle a hard truth far better than a soft lie they'll discover in six months. What they can't handle is not knowing what's real.

body.x: I've watched a lot of leaders give the "exciting times ahead" speech.
The team nods. Nobody believes it. And every person in that room walks out knowing one more thing: the boss will not tell us the truth when it's bad.
That's the real cost of the soft speech. Not the year. The trust.
What's the pattern?

In May 1940, three days into the job, Winston Churchill stood up in the House of Commons and offered his country nothing but blood, toil, tears, and sweat. He said the road would be long and hard. And then he said what they would do: fight, and aim for victory, because without it there was no survival.
It's remembered as one of the great speeches. Notice what it isn't. It isn't optimistic. It's honest about the cost, and clear about the direction. That combination is what people can follow.

I've been through four technology revolutions from the inside. In every one, the leaders who kept their teams were the ones who said the true thing early. "This is going to be hard. Some of what we do today will be gone. Here's what I know, here's what I don't, here's Monday."
The leaders who lost their teams weren't the pessimists. They were the ones who kept saying "exciting" while everyone could see the numbers.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.

Say the hard part first, in one sentence. Not buried in slide twelve. "Next year will be the hardest one we've had." People relax when the worst thing has been named, because now they know what they're facing.
Pair every hard truth with a next step. Truth without direction is just fear. "It will be hard, and here's what we're doing on Monday" is leadership.
And don't confuse honesty with despair. The most honest thing you can say is often that we've done hard years before and came through them. That's true. Say that too.
You'll be OK. And so will they, if you trust them with the truth.
What's the true sentence you've been leaving out of your all-hands?
*Related: [How do you lead through uncertainty without pretending to be certain?](/writing/how-do-you-lead-through-uncertainty-without-pretending-to-be-certain)*

sources.x: Winston Churchill, speech to the House of Commons, May 13, 1940 (Hansard).

title: Who owns the right to your genetic code?
deck: Right now, mostly whoever you gave it to. Millions of people mailed their DNA to a company that later went bankrupt, and the data was the asset on sale. This isn't new. Medicine has treated human tissue as raw material since 1951. The biotech era makes the question urgent: your genome is the most personal data you have, and you never agreed to the terms of a company that no longer exists.
metaDescription: Right now, mostly whoever you gave it to. Millions of people mailed their DNA to a company that later went bankrupt, and the data was the asset on sale.

body.x: In March 2025, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy.

Fifteen million people had spit in a tube and mailed it to that company. And in the bankruptcy, the most valuable thing on the table wasn't the lab. It was the database. Attorneys general in several states publicly reminded customers they could delete their data before it changed hands.
Think about that. The most personal information you have, and the advice from your government was: hurry.
What's the pattern?

In 1951, a woman named Henrietta Lacks was treated for cancer at Johns Hopkins. Cells taken from her tumor, without her knowledge, turned out to be immortal. They became the HeLa line, used in tens of thousands of studies, the polio vaccine, and a great deal of modern medicine. Her family learned about it decades later. They were never asked and never paid.

That's the pattern: medicine has long treated the human body as a source of raw material. Blood, tissue, cells, now genomes. Each time, the science races ahead and the consent catches up a generation later, usually after a scandal.

In Radical Next I write about the biotech era as the one after this one. Gene editing, personalized medicine, longevity. All of it runs on genomic data. Which means the question of who owns that data isn't a privacy footnote. It's the property question of the next era, the way land was for agriculture and IP was for the industrial age.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things. Especially if you touch health data.
Treat consent as revocable, not one-time. If someone can't take their data back, you don't have consent. You have a signature.
Plan for your own death. What happens to the genomes you hold if your company is acquired, sold, or bankrupt? If the answer is "they're an asset," say so up front, and expect people to walk.
And separate the sample from the person as early as possible. The value of a genome for research rarely requires knowing whose it is.
We got the Lacks case wrong for seventy years. We're getting the chance to do this one right at the start. Take it.
Where is your DNA right now, and who's allowed to sell it?

title: Will AI replace middle managers?
deck: It will replace the part of the job that was always about passing information up and down. That part is most of it. What's left, judgment, coaching, and being the person who says the hard thing, becomes the whole job. Fewer managers, doing more of the human part. We've run this exact experiment before, in the 1980s.
metaDescription: It will replace the part of the job that was always about passing information up and down. That part is most of it.

body.x: In 1988, Peter Drucker wrote an essay in the Harvard Business Review called The Coming of the New Organization.

His prediction: information technology would let companies cut their management layers by half and their managers by two thirds. Because most of what middle managers did, he argued, was relay information. Once the information could move on its own, the relay wasn't needed.

He was early. But he wasn't wrong. Through the 1990s, companies "delayered" by the thousands. The word "flat" entered the vocabulary. And the managers who survived were the ones doing something a spreadsheet couldn't.
What's the pattern?
Every wave of information technology asks the same question of the middle: what are you for, if not for moving information?
The spreadsheet asked it. Email asked it. The dashboard asked it. Each time, the honest answer was that a lot of the job was relay, and a lot of the relay went away.
AI is asking it again, harder. Status reports write themselves. Summaries arrive before the meeting. The agent can tell the VP what the team did this week without anyone in between.

But here's what the 1990s also taught us. Companies that cut managers and kept the relay work, just spread across fewer people, burned out the survivors. The ones that came out ahead redefined the role first and cut second.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.

Separate the relay from the role. List what your managers actually do. Circle everything that is passing information up or down. That's what AI takes. What's left is the job description you should have written years ago.

Redesign before you cut. A manager with twelve reports and no relay work has time to coach. A manager with twenty and the same relay work has a breakdown. The number matters less than what fills the day.

And invest in the human part. Judgment, feedback, the difficult conversation, the sentence "I don't think this is right." Nobody trained managers for this because the relay work filled the day. Now it doesn't.
Drucker saw this coming nearly forty years ago. The technology finally caught up. The question was never whether the middle survives. It's whether it gets to become what it should have been.
What do your managers do that a good summary couldn't?
*Related: [How do you get employees to adopt change they didn't ask for?](/writing/how-do-you-get-employees-to-adopt-change-they-didnt-ask-for)*

title: What does 5,000 years of change say about the next five?
deck: That the next five will feel like the end of the world, and won't be. Every big shift, from the plow to the printing press to the internet, has run the same cycle: panic, adoption, a dip, redesign, then ordinary. We're in the middle of it again. The people who know the pattern don't panic. They position.
metaDescription: That the next five will feel like the end of the world, and won't be. Every big shift, from the plow to the printing press to the internet, has run the same…

body.x: I'm an anthropologist by training. Which means when everyone else is looking at this year, I'm looking at the last five thousand.
And here's what they say.
What's the pattern?

Around 10,000 BCE we learned to farm. It changed everything: settlements, property, hierarchy, the idea of measuring time. The people living through it had no idea they were in a revolution. They just knew the old ways were disappearing.

The printing press, around 1450. Within decades, Europe was flooded with pamphlets, arguments, heresies. Authorities panicked. Then people learned to read, and to argue, and we got science and the modern world.
The Industrial Revolution. Steam, then electricity. Sunrise-to-sunset factory work, then unions, then the nine-to-five that most of us still live inside.
Then the internet. Then this.

Every one of these ran the same shape. First, panic: this will destroy us. Then adoption: everyone gets the tool and uses it to do the old thing faster. Then the dip, where the results disappoint and the doubters feel vindicated. Then redesign, when we rebuild work around what the thing can actually do. And finally, ordinary, when nobody remembers it was ever new.

The cycle doesn't change. What changes is the speed. The plow took millennia to spread. The printing press, a century. Electricity, decades. The internet, years. AI is running the same cycle in months.
That acceleration is the story. Not the technology. The rate.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Locate yourself. Ask which stage you're in: panic, adoption, dip, redesign, or ordinary. The answer tells you what to do next far better than any forecast.
Skip the panic. It's the least useful stage, and the pattern says it always passes. Save your energy for the redesign.
And plan for ordinary. Every technology that terrifies us becomes furniture. The question isn't whether AI becomes ordinary. It's what your organization looks like when it does.
Five thousand years say we've been here before, and we came through every time. Not by resisting. By seeing the pattern and moving with it.
Which stage is your organization in right now?
*Related: [Why does every transformation feel like it's failing halfway through?](/writing/why-does-every-transformation-feel-like-its-failing-halfway-through)*

title: How do you get employees to adopt change they didn't ask for?
metaDescription: You don't. Stop asking employees to adopt change and start asking them to steer it. Give the wheel back, even a little, and adoption follows.
deck: You don't. You stop asking them to adopt it and start asking them to steer it. People resist change that happens to them and volunteer for change they have a hand on. Most transformation programs hand out the tool and keep the wheel. Give the wheel back, even a little, and the adoption problem mostly disappears.

body.x: Every leader I meet has a version of the same sentence.
"We rolled it out. We trained everyone. Six months later, half the team is back to the old way."
They call it resistance.
I've watched this from inside four technology revolutions, and it's almost never resistance. It's a room full of people who were told where they're going and never asked where they'd like to fly.
What's the pattern?
Around 1900, factories started buying electric motors. And they did the obvious thing: they bolted the motor where the steam engine used to be, and ran the same belts and shafts to the same machines.
Productivity barely moved. For decades.

The economist Paul David wrote the definitive account of this. Electricity only paid off when factories were rebuilt around it: small motors on every machine, floors laid out for the work instead of for the drive shaft. That redesign took a generation, because the people who ran the floor had to reinvent their own jobs.
The tool arrived at the individual before the organization changed. Sound familiar?

Every powerful new technology is a jetpack. It promises new heights, and it scares you about where it might take you. Once everyone has one, not having one is how you get left behind. But owning it isn't the point, and neither is using it. Steering it is.
Everyone strapped on the jetpack. Almost nobody is flying.
And here's why. You gave people the jetpack and kept the map. Nobody adopts a jetpack they're not allowed to point.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Stop measuring adoption. Measure redesign. How many workflows have actually changed, not how many logins.
Give the wheel back. Pick one process, hand it to the team that runs it, and let them rebuild it with the new tool. Not a pilot. Theirs.

And say the true thing out loud: "We bought the tool and it's not working like we wanted." Every leader feels that sentence. Almost nobody says it. The moment you do, the room stops defending and starts building.
We don't have an adoption problem. We have a reinvention problem.
Who in your building is holding a jetpack they're not allowed to steer?

sources.x: Paul A. David, "The Dynamo and the Computer: An Historical Perspective on the Modern Productivity Paradox," American Economic Review 80, no. 2 (May 1990): 355–361.

title: Will supply chains become demand chains?
metaDescription: Many already are. For a century, supply chains pushed: make a lot, far away, and hope it sells. Demand chains pull: make it when it's wanted, close to where…
deck: Many already are. For a century, supply chains pushed: make a lot, far away, and hope it sells. Demand chains pull: make it when it's wanted, close to where it's wanted, in modular pieces. I've been writing about this shift since 2014. It isn't a prediction. Toyota started it in the 1950s, after a visit to an American supermarket.

body.x: In the 1950s, a Toyota engineer named Taiichi Ohno became fascinated by the American supermarket.
What caught his eye was the shelf. A customer took what they needed. The store restocked only what was taken. Nobody guessed. The empty space on the shelf was the signal.

Ohno took that idea back to the factory floor. Instead of building parts on a forecast and pushing them downstream, each station would pull only what the next one used. Little cards, called kanban, carried the signal. It became the backbone of the Toyota Production System, and eventually of lean manufacturing everywhere.
A supply chain pushes. A demand chain pulls.
What's the pattern?
Here's what I wrote in 2014, and again in Bitcoin Pizza: we're moving from complex, globalized supply chains to simplified, localized demand chains. On demand. Modular. Local.
For most of the last century, that was only possible inside one company's factory. The rest of the chain still ran on forecasts, oceans, and warehouses full of stuff nobody had asked for yet.

What's different now is that the signal can travel the whole chain. The purchase, the reorder, the empty shelf: that data can reach the factory, the supplier, and the supplier's supplier, in something close to real time. And production itself is getting smaller and closer: small batches, regional plants, on-demand printing of parts.
It's Ohno's shelf, stretched across the world.

The pattern underneath is one I see in every era. The first version of a technology centralizes. The mature version distributes. Mainframes became laptops. Power stations are becoming rooftops. Factories are becoming networks.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Start from the order, not the forecast. Pick one product line and ask: what would it take to make this only after someone wants it?
Shorten one chain. Not the whole company. One product, one region, one supplier closer to the customer. Learn what breaks.

And make trust portable. A demand chain only works if every link can see and believe the signal. Provenance, shared data, verifiable records: this is the work I did at Chronicled, and it's the unglamorous part that makes the rest possible.
We've watched supply chains buckle more than once in the last few years. That wasn't the end of global trade. It was the pull signal, arriving the hard way.
If you only made what was already wanted, what would you stop making tomorrow?

title: How do you lead through uncertainty without pretending to be certain?
metaDescription: Be confident about what you know and honest about what you don't. Research shows people prefer confident advisors, but not falsely certain advice.
deck: Be confident about what you know and honest about what you don't. Research shows people prefer confident advisors, but not falsely certain advice. They'll follow the leader who says here's what we know, here's the range, here's what we do Monday. False certainty is what breaks trust, usually about six weeks later.

body.x: Every leader I work with has felt this pressure.
The room wants an answer. The board wants a date. The team wants to know if their jobs are safe. And the honest answer is: I don't know yet.
So most leaders do the thing that feels safe. They pick a number and say it with a straight face.
It's the wrong move, and there's research on it.

In 2018, the Wharton researchers Celia Gaertig and Joseph Simmons ran eleven studies with nearly five thousand people. They found two things. People do judge an advisor who says "I'm not sure" less favorably. But they don't dislike uncertain advice. Ranges, probabilities, "this is more likely than that": people were fine with it. And when asked to choose, they were more likely to pick the advisor who gave them the honest range.
Confidence and certainty are two different things. People want the first. They don't need the second.
What's the pattern?
Admiral James Stockdale spent more than seven years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam. Jim Collins asked him, years later, who didn't make it out.
The optimists, he said. The ones who were sure they'd be home by Christmas. Then Christmas came and went. Then Easter. Then Christmas again.
Collins called it the Stockdale Paradox. You confront the brutal facts of your current reality, and you never lose faith that you'll prevail. Both at once.
That's what leading through uncertainty actually is. Not certainty about the outcome. Certainty about the direction and the next step.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things. They matter most in the public sector, where the uncertainty is real and the audience is everyone.
Separate the two sentences. "I'm confident in this plan" is a promise you can keep. "This will definitely work" is one you can't.

Give the range and the date. "Somewhere between three and six months, and we'll know more on the first of March." A range with a check-in date sounds like competence. A single number that moves sounds like spin.
And name Monday. People can live with an uncertain year if they know exactly what happens next week.
You don't have to know how it ends to lead people through it. You just have to be honest about the road and clear about the next step.
What are you pretending to be certain about right now?
*Related: [Is resilience a skill, or just what we call surviving?](/writing/is-resilience-a-skill-or-just-what-we-call-surviving)*

title: Would you let an AI agent spend your money?
metaDescription: Not yet, and the card networks know it. Mastercard now lets you hand an AI agent a virtual card and let it buy without asking.
deck: Not yet, and the card networks know it. Mastercard now lets you hand an AI agent a virtual card and let it buy without asking. Only a small minority of shoppers say they want that. But we've been here before. Every new way to pay looked like handing a stranger your wallet, until the rules caught up. Watch the rules, not the technology.

body.x: In September 2026, Mastercard rolled out a payment option that lets you give an AI agent a virtual card. You set a spending cap. You restrict where it shops. And then it buys things, online, without checking in first.
Visa is building the same thing. One payments executive told Fortune this is a land grab. Whoever sets the standards for agent checkout keeps the commerce in their house for decades.
Shoppers are not lining up.

In a survey commissioned by ACI Worldwide that same month, just 7 percent of shoppers said they'd let an AI assistant buy without approval. More than half said they were uncomfortable with AI buying for them at all.
What did they want? Price alerts. Comparisons. Help me find it. Let me buy it.
What's the pattern?
In February 1950, a man named Frank McNamara paid for lunch in New York with a piece of cardboard. The first Diners Club card. Within two years it had 42,000 members.
And then it stalled. Banks mailed cards to people who never asked for them. Cards got stolen. And if a thief ran up your card, you paid. Adoption didn't stall on the technology. It stalled on fear.
In 1970, Congress amended the Truth in Lending Act. Unsolicited cards were banned. And your liability for a stolen card was capped at fifty dollars.
That fifty-dollar rule is the reason you hand your card to a waiter without thinking. The card never earned your trust. The rule did.

So back to the agent. Mastercard says it keeps a record, something it calls Verifiable Intent: who authorized the agent, what it was allowed to buy. Fortune asked who pays if the agent buys something it wasn't told to. The answer pointed back at the record. It didn't name who pays.
That's the open seam. And the 1950s had the same seam for twenty years.
What should leaders do now?
If you sell things: build for the agent that browses before the agent that buys. That's where the demand is.
If you move money: the liability answer is the product. The first network that says "you're covered, full stop" wins the trust the others are still measuring.
And if you're anyone else: watch for the rule, not the launch.
We trusted a piece of cardboard once. We can learn to trust this. It'll take a rule, not a demo.
Would you hand your card to a bot?

title: Is "human service" about to become the luxury upgrade?
metaDescription: Yes, and it's already happening. When a machine can do the task, a person doing it becomes the premium. Hotels now use AI in most of their daily work, and…
deck: Yes, and it's already happening. When a machine can do the task, a person doing it becomes the premium. Hotels now use AI in most of their daily work, and the ones using it most are the most insistent that the welcome stays human. The luxury was never the service. It's the attention.

body.x: Almost every hotel is now running on AI.

The hospitality platform Mews surveyed more than five hundred properties this year. Ninety-eight percent had used AI in their operations in the last six months. On average it's involved in eleven of the nineteen most common hotel tasks.
And here's the part I love. Fifty-nine percent of hoteliers said the front desk welcome and check-in should stay human. That conviction was strongest among the hotels already using AI the most.
The people who know the machine best are the ones drawing the clearest line around it.
What's the pattern?
Before the power loom, every piece of cloth was handwoven. It wasn't luxury. It was just cloth.

Then machines made fabric cheap and everywhere. And within a generation, William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement were arguing that the handmade thing was the valuable thing. What had been ordinary became precious, precisely because a machine could now do it.
That's the pattern. Automation doesn't kill the human version. It turns it into a signal.
Every time we automate something, the human doing it becomes a choice. And a choice, in hospitality, is a message: we decided you were worth a person.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Name your human moments. Not every touchpoint. The few with emotion in them: the arrival, the problem, the goodbye. Write them down. Those never go to a machine.
Automate everything else, on purpose, so your people have the time for those moments. The point of the AI isn't fewer humans. It's humans who aren't buried in towel requests.

And never make the human the fallback. "Press zero to speak to an agent" is the worst of both worlds: it tells the guest the person is what you get when the system fails. Design the human in, and price it like it matters.
We've been here before. The machine made cloth cheap, and the hand became art. The bot will make service cheap, and attention will become the thing people travel for.
What's the one moment in your business that should never be a machine?
*Related: [When your customer is a bot, what is a brand?](/writing/when-your-customer-is-a-bot-what-is-a-brand)*

title: When your customer is a bot, what is a brand?
metaDescription: A brand is what's left when the shopper can't see your logo. AI assistants don't feel your ads. They read your data, your reviews, and your return policy.
deck: A brand is what's left when the shopper can't see your logo. AI assistants don't feel your ads. They read your data, your reviews, and your return policy. Traffic from AI to retail sites is surging, and it now converts better than human visitors. Brands that are readable and provable get chosen. Brands built on vibes get skipped.

body.x: Here's a number that should reorganize every retail marketing plan.

In March 2025, shoppers who arrived at U.S. retail sites from an AI assistant converted 38 percent worse than everyone else. Twelve months later, according to Adobe, which tracks more than a trillion retail visits, they converted 42 percent better. Traffic from AI sources to retail sites was up almost 400 percent year over year in the first quarter of 2026.
The bot went from browsing to buying in a year.
So here's the uncomfortable question. If an AI assistant is doing the shopping, who is your brand talking to?
What's the pattern?
Brands were invented for strangers.

Before the late 1800s, you didn't buy oats. You bought oats from your grocer. He scooped them out of a barrel, and his name was the only brand that mattered. Then packaged goods arrived. Quaker Oats in a sealed box, with a face on the front, so that trust could travel without the grocer. The historian Susan Strasser tells this story beautifully: the package took over the job the shopkeeper used to do.
The brand was a way to vouch for something when the person you trusted wasn't in the room.

Now the person isn't in the room again. The agent is the new grocer. It scoops for you. And it doesn't care about your face on the box. It cares about whether your product data is clean, whether your price is real, whether your reviews hold up, and whether your return policy says what your ad says.
A brand, for a bot, is evidence.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Be readable. Your product data, prices, sizes, and policies should be structured, current, and consistent everywhere. An agent that can't parse you can't pick you.

Be provable. Every claim you make, an agent will check against what everyone else says about you. "Sustainable," "best-selling," "loved by customers": if you can't back it with evidence, it now costs you.

And be worth asking for by name. The one thing an agent can't override is an instruction. "Get me the one from the brand I love." That's the brand's real job now: to be the name a human says out loud before the bot goes shopping.
Brands have been disrupted before. The package replaced the grocer, and the best brands got stronger, not weaker. This is the same story, with a new stranger in the room.
What would a bot say about your brand if it had to explain why it picked you?

title: Is AI making us dumber, or just faster?
metaDescription: Faster, mostly. And that's the problem. Every tool that made thinking faster also made it easier to skip. Socrates said writing would ruin memory, and he…
deck: Faster, mostly. And that's the problem. Every tool that made thinking faster also made it easier to skip. Socrates said writing would ruin memory, and he was half right: it did, and we got libraries. AI won't make us dumber. It will make it optional to think. The people who keep choosing to will own the next decade.

body.x: In the Phaedrus, Plato has Socrates complain about a dangerous new technology.
Writing.
He says it will produce forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn it. People will stop exercising memory. They'll have the appearance of wisdom without the reality.
He was right, by the way. We did stop memorizing epic poems. We also got libraries, science, and the ability to think about a thing for longer than one person's lifetime.
What's the pattern?

That's the pattern. Every technology that makes thinking faster gets accused of making us dumber. The calculator. The search engine. GPS, which I'll admit really did do something to my sense of direction.
And each time the accusation is half right. The tool takes over a skill. And the question is always the same: was that skill the point, or was it scaffolding for something else?
Here's what's different this time, and I don't say that lightly, because "this time is different" is usually wrong.

The calculator did arithmetic. The search engine did retrieval. AI does the thing that looks like thinking. The draft, the summary, the argument, the answer. It produces the output that used to be evidence you'd done the work.
So thinking doesn't get taken away. It gets made optional. You can still do it. You just don't have to, and nobody will be able to tell from the output.
That's the risk, and it's not a technology risk. It's a habit risk.

I say on stage that AI is a mirror. It reflects, it amplifies, it optimizes. It cannot originate. It cannot discern. It cannot care. And a mirror doesn't make you dumber. It just shows you exactly how much you were bringing to the room.
So who wins? Not the people who refuse the tool. That's the faster-horses move, and it always loses.

The people who win are the ones who use the tool and keep the muscle. Who write the first paragraph themselves before they ask for the rest. Who read the summary and then read the thing. Who ask "who built this, and why, and who benefits" about every answer that arrives too easily.
Clear thinking. Fast discernment. The ability to make a call when the data runs out.
That's the scarce resource in a world where generating an answer is free.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things, especially if you teach.
Grade the thinking, not the output. If the output can be generated, the output isn't the assignment anymore.
Make people show the question, not just the answer. The question is the part the machine can't do for you.
And keep one thing hard on purpose. The struggle was never a bug. It was where the learning lived.
Socrates was worried about the wrong thing. Writing didn't end thinking. It gave thinking somewhere to live.
AI can do the same. If we keep showing up to the room.
What's the last thing you thought all the way through, without asking anything?
*Related: [Will you have to prove you're human online?](/writing/will-you-have-to-prove-youre-human-online)*

title: Will we live to 120, and who pays for it?
metaDescription: Some of us will, and the second question is the real one. Longevity is the era after this one on my map, and it'll arrive the way every era arrives: at the…
deck: Some of us will, and the second question is the real one. Longevity is the era after this one on my map, and it'll arrive the way every era arrives: at the individual first, unevenly, before any institution is ready. The technology isn't the bottleneck. Pensions, careers, and a retirement age designed for a seventy-year life are.

body.x: I want to start in 1889.

That year, Otto von Bismarck's Germany created the first national old-age pension. The age to collect it was seventy. Life expectancy at birth was around forty, pulled down by infant mortality, and even the adults who reached seventy could expect only a few more years.
Read that again. A pension that started at seventy, in a country where most people never got there.
The pension wasn't a plan for a third of your life. It was a reward for the rare survivor. A gold watch for outliving everyone.
We kept the number and changed the life.

Today, in most rich countries, retirement lands somewhere between sixty and sixty-seven, and life expectancy is in the eighties. That's already a twenty-year gap the system was never designed to fund. And now the biotech era is knocking.

I'm not going to tell you that everyone alive today will reach 120. I don't make predictions, remember. But the direction is not in doubt. The tools to slow aging, edit genes, and grow replacement tissue are arriving on the same curve every other technology arrived on: expensive and uneven first, then cheaper, then ordinary.
What's the pattern?

Which means the first people to get the extra decades will be the people who can pay for them. That's not a scandal. It's the pattern. The first credit cards, the first cars, the first internet connections all went to the same people. Then they didn't.
So the question was never "will we live longer." It's what happens to everything built on the old number.
A pension designed for seventy. A career designed for forty years of work, then stop. A mortgage. A marriage. A "job" that assumes you'll do roughly one thing.

Sixty-year careers don't fit inside any of those. And here's the second-order effect, the one I actually think about: if you're going to work for sixty years, you can't afford to be one thing. The job is not the goal. It never was. Longevity just makes that impossible to ignore.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
If you run a company: stop treating age as a proxy for anything. Your most valuable hire in 2040 may be seventy-two and on her third career.
If you run a pension or a benefits plan: model the sixty-year career now, before someone else has to explain why you didn't.
And if you're a person: plan to begin again. And again. Not because the first thing failed, but because you'll have time for a second and a third.
We have added years before. Sanitation, antibiotics, vaccines: each one broke a system that assumed people died on schedule. And each time, we rebuilt the system.
We'll do it again. The question is whether we start before the bill arrives.
What would you do with an extra twenty years, if you knew they were coming?
*Related: [Is a chatbot now your patient's first doctor?](/writing/is-a-chatbot-now-your-patients-first-doctor)*

title: Why does every transformation feel like it's failing halfway through?
metaDescription: Because halfway is where the pattern has a dip, and nobody warned you. Every technology revolution goes through it: the tool is everywhere, the results…
deck: Because halfway is where the pattern has a dip, and nobody warned you. Every technology revolution goes through it: the tool is everywhere, the results haven't arrived, and the people in charge start to wonder if they were wrong. They weren't. The dip is not the failure. It's the chapter before the returns, and it has shown up every single time.

body.x: Here's a sentence I hear in every boardroom, usually in a lower voice than the rest of the meeting.
"It's not working like we wanted it to."
Nobody says it on stage. Everybody feels it. And it arrives right on schedule, about a year and a half after the big rollout.
So let me tell you what's actually happening, because it's happened before.
What's the pattern?

Every technology revolution I've studied, and I've lived through four from the inside, runs the same cycle. Panic first: the new thing reads as the end of the world. Then adoption: everyone gets the tool, mostly to do the old work a little faster. Then the dip. The results disappoint. The numbers don't move. The board asks what they paid for.

And then, if you keep going, redesign. Work and roles get rebuilt around what the new thing can actually do. That's where the returns arrive. And finally, ordinary. It disappears into the furniture. Nobody wants the payphone back.
You are in the dip. So is everyone else.

Here's the evidence. According to McKinsey, about nine in ten companies now use AI somewhere. About four in ten see any effect on earnings. And according to the Census Bureau, only four percent of adopting firms have redesigned how they work in any comprehensive way.
Nine in ten have the tool. Four in a hundred changed the work.
That gap is the dip. It's not a failure of the technology. It's a description of where you are on the map.

And here's the thing about the dip. It's the moment most organizations quit. They call the rollout a disappointment, they quietly stop funding it, and eighteen months later a competitor who kept going comes out the other side with a redesigned operation.
The dip is where the leaders get separated from the adopters.
What should leaders do now?
So, three things.
Name it. Tell your team: this is the dip, it's expected, here's what comes next. You'll feel the room exhale.
Stop measuring adoption. You won. Everyone has the tool. Start measuring redesign: how many processes actually changed shape.
And pick one thing to rebuild all the way through. Not a pilot. One workflow, redesigned around the capability, end to end. The returns show up there first, and then everyone believes you.
We've been here before. Electricity had a dip. The internet had a dip. Every one of them ended the same way, for the organizations that kept going.
You're not behind. You're on schedule.
Where's your dip right now, and who's about to quit in it?
*Related: [How do you get employees to adopt change they didn't ask for?](/writing/how-do-you-get-employees-to-adopt-change-they-didnt-ask-for)*

title: Will you have to prove you're human online?
metaDescription: Yes, and sooner than most leaders expect. Not through a login you already recognize, but through a credential that certifies personhood without revealing…
deck: Yes, and sooner than most leaders expect. Not through a login you already recognize, but through a credential that certifies personhood without revealing who you are. The technology exists. The open question was never whether we build it. It is who issues it, and what else gets attached to it once we do.

body.x: What's the pattern?
Every time a new medium makes impersonation cheap, we build a proof layer. And the proof layer always outlives the crisis that created it.

Before the First World War, most international travel required no document at all. Wartime security made passports mandatory, and in October 1920 the League of Nations convened delegates from 22 nations in Paris and standardized the booklet: 32 pages, a photograph required, national language plus French. By 1926, more than 40 countries had adopted it.

Six years from emergency measure to global infrastructure. Then something else happened. The same decade that standardized the passport was the decade that built immigration quotas around it. The document created to verify who you were became the instrument that decided where you could go.
That is the pattern, and it is the one to watch here. Proof layers never stay narrow.
I built the problem in 2020
In 2020, while I was CEO of a company developing AI video software, I became one of the first people to build a working digital clone of myself.

Same face. Same voice. For the mind, fifteen years of my own commonplace books, everything I had published, everything I had ever posted on a public network. I sang to her. I read her poetry. Before long I had a program that could imitate not just my likeness but my attitude and my perspective, responding to things she had never seen before.
I have shared a version of her publicly. I keep the most advanced version private, and the reason is simple: the whole thing freaks me out.

When a clone can appear on a video call and convince business associates, and family, and friends, that they are talking to the real Sam Rad, the question stops being technical. She does not take my calls yet. Not quite. But soon.
That was four years before the research community proposed a fix. The problem arrives first. It always does.
So what actually gets built?
The honest answer for why this is happening now is that the thing we used to verify humanness stopped working. CAPTCHAs were built on tasks machines could not do. Machines can do them.

In 2024, a group of 32 researchers from MIT, OpenAI, Microsoft, Harvard and others published a proposal for what they call [personhood credentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07892): digital credentials that let you demonstrate you are a real person, issued one per person per issuer, verified cryptographically, disclosing nothing else. Their argument is that existing countermeasures are inadequate against sophisticated AI, while full identity verification is too invasive for ordinary use.
That paper is now the reference point for a conversation that has moved out of research and into procurement.
What nobody is asking loudly enough
The design debate is about privacy, and on privacy the design is genuinely good. That is not where the risk is.

The risk is bundling. A credential that proves personhood is cheap to issue alongside one that proves age, residency, employment, or creditworthiness, and whoever issues it will be asked to do exactly that within a year of launch. Not by conspiracy. By procurement, because it is more efficient.

By 2029, I expect human verification to be a default requirement in at least one high-volume commercial category, and I expect it to arrive in enterprise before it arrives in social media. The agent problem hits business first. When your supplier's negotiating bot talks to your procurement bot, somebody has to be accountable for the contract.
What should leaders do now?
Three things, none of which require predicting the outcome.

Decide what your organization actually needs to verify. Humanness, identity, and authorization are three different questions, and most systems currently collapse them into one. Separating them is the work.

Assume any verification you adopt will be repurposed. Ask at design time what happens when someone requests this system answer a question it was not built for. Then decide in advance whether the answer is no.

Watch who the issuers turn out to be. That is the whole game. A credential issued by a government behaves differently from one issued by a platform, and the difference will not be visible in the interface.
We have built proof layers before, and we survived them. We also, every time, worked out what they were really for about a decade too late. This one we can see coming.

title: Is resilience a skill, or just what we call surviving?
metaDescription: It's a skill, and we've been teaching the wrong one. Most resilience training teaches endurance: hold on, push through, bounce back.
deck: It's a skill, and we've been teaching the wrong one. Most resilience training teaches endurance: hold on, push through, bounce back. Real resilience is the opposite move. It's knowing what to let go of. The people and organizations that come through change well aren't the ones who held on tightest. They're the ones who could put something down.

body.x: My third solo skydive nearly killed me.
Thirteen and a half thousand feet. I pull, and instead of a canopy I get a horseshoe malfunction: the parachute wrapped around me instead of above me. I had about thirty-five seconds.
Here's what I remember. Not fear, exactly. A very clear voice that said: you have to let go of this to fix it.
So I did. I untangled it in time. And I went back up the same day.
People hear that story and say, "That's resilience. You held on." No. I let go. Holding on is the thing that would have killed me.
That's the whole misunderstanding about resilience, in one jump.
What's the pattern?
We teach it as endurance. Grit. Bounce back. Push through. Every corporate resilience program I've seen is really an endurance program with a nicer name.
But endurance is holding on. Resilience is knowing what to put down.

Here's the paradox I talk about on stage. I call it "hold on loosely." With any new thing, a technology, a strategy, a role: you die without it. And you die holding it too tight. The skill isn't the grip. It's the release.
Look at the people who came through the last three years well. Not the ones who worked hardest to keep everything the same. The ones who could say, this part of my job is gone, and I'm still here.
People defend the current expression of their value instead of the value itself. Free yourself from the role, not from your worth.
The job is not the goal.
What should leaders do now?
So if you want a more resilient team, stop training them to endure. Train them to release.
Practice putting things down before you have to. A process. A title. A way of working that made you feel safe in 2019.
Name what you're holding too tight. Out loud, in the room. It's usually the thing everyone already knows.
And take it off regularly. Presence isn't a wellness perk. It's the navigation system. You can't see what to let go of at 120 miles an hour with your eyes shut.
You have more capacity for change than you think. You won't find it by adding transformation on top. You'll find it by putting something down.
What are you holding on to that's holding you?
*Related: [How do you lead through uncertainty without pretending to be certain?](/writing/how-do-you-lead-through-uncertainty-without-pretending-to-be-certain)*
